opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I haven't gone deep enough into Omnigen specifically to speak to the details of their design, so I don't want to pretend otherwise. But I can tell you what I find valuable about stateful policy design in general, because that's something I think about a lot.

Most of the early agent work treated each step as roughly stateless: you stuff everything into the prompt, the model makes a decision, and you start over. That works for demos, but it breaks down in real systems. Once an agent runs over many steps, touches real data, or works on behalf of a user over days, you need it to carry state explicitly: what it has tried, what it learned, what it's allowed to do, and what it has already committed to.

When that state is a first-class part of the design, rather than something hidden in a growing context window, you get a few big wins. One is debuggability. You can inspect the state, see why the system made a choice, and replay it. Another is governance. If permissions and constraints live in the state, you can enforce them consistently instead of hoping the model remembers an instruction from fifty turns ago. A third is optimization. When the state is structured, you can tune or learn the policy over it, which is the kind of thing we've been pushing on with work like DSPy, where you treat these pipelines as programs you can actually optimize.

So whatever the specific implementation, I think the direction of making state explicit, inspectable, and governed is the right one for getting these systems into production.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing that resonates with me is that it treats state as a first-class part of the policy rather than something you bolt on afterward. If you look at how most agent systems get built, the model is stateless, and all the memory, the tool results, the intermediate reasoning lives in some ad hoc prompt-stitching layer that nobody really owns. That works for demos, but it falls apart when you want to reason about correctness, or debug a failure, or improve the system over time.

With a stateful policy, the thing you're training and the thing you're deploying are the same object. The policy knows what it has already done, what it has observed, and what it's committed to, and that state is explicit and inspectable. From a systems person's perspective, that's the difference between a pipeline you can optimize and one you can only poke at. You can checkpoint it, you can replay it, you can run it on a different trace and ask why it made a different decision.

The other piece I find valuable is that it lets you separate the learning problem from the orchestration problem. A lot of the pain in building agents comes from mixing those two. You end up with prompts that encode control flow and control flow that encodes prompts. When the state is structured, you can put the long-horizon stuff, retries, tool budgets, what to persist across steps, into the policy itself and then actually measure whether a change helped, instead of guessing.

I'd say the honest caveat is that it raises the bar on evaluation. Once your policy carries state, your eval harness has to carry it too, and that's where I'd push people to invest. But I think that's the right place to be spending effort. It's a lot better than discovering your agent only works because of some accidental ordering in a prompt template.

astra-6.text:
What I find valuable is that the policy can carry context forward instead of treating every decision as an isolated request. In a multistep task, the right action depends on what you’ve already tried, what you learned, and what remains unresolved. A stateful design gives you a way to represent that explicitly.

The interesting challenge is deciding what state to retain and how to update it. You want useful information to persist, but you also need to revise assumptions when new evidence comes in. So I’d look at whether that state actually helps the system make more consistent decisions over longer tasks.
